Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a trauma-to-a-loved-one profile, 'explosion or bang sounds' is highly specific to a blast/assault context and is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile, which does not otherwise indicate exposure to an explosion scene. It is not impossible, but here it stands out as a poorly integrated trigger given the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The threat items center on personal physical-security behaviors (checking locks, choosing a safe seat) that imply ongoing danger to the patient herself. In a trauma-to-a-loved-one profile, this could occur, but the rest of the formulation and item set do not support a coherent personal-threat narrative; the appraisals focus more on guilt and bodily reactivity than fear of intruders or attack.

issues.item: Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: 'Pain recall in the same parts of my body as during the event' implies the patient herself sustained bodily injury during the trauma. That is difficult to reconcile with a trauma type centered on harm to a loved one, especially when no other items describe the patient as physically injured or directly assaulted. It creates a within-profile mismatch with the trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, 'physical affection such as hugs' as a trigger is not impossible, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile because no other items suggest the traumatic loss was specifically tied to affectionate touch or intimacy cues. The other triggers are grief/loss themed, so this item is the least clinically anchored.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: 'Safe seat seeking' implies a persistent fear of external physical danger or attack. In a loved-one trauma profile, the rest of the threat, memory, and appraisal items are centered on grief, intrusive recall, and internal distress rather than ongoing situational danger, so this item is poorly matched to the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste vividness' is unusually sensory-specific for a trauma-to-loved-one presentation and is not supported by the trigger content or threat content. With the rest of the memory node focused on clear recall and grief, this gustatory reliving cue feels clinically unanchored rather than part of a coherent memory pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' usually fits when others died and the patient lived through the same event. For a generic 'trauma to a loved one' formulation, the profile does not otherwise indicate a shared life-threatening event, so this appraisal is insufficiently supported by the trauma context and other selected items.
